A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MA-GTS and G-REAL. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, node-size analyses, inference-cost measurements, and layer ablations for MA-GTS.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds task and model evaluations, repeated-query measurements, larger-graph experiments, and runtime comparisons.

M1.justification: The three-layer architecture, six agents, algorithm selection, tool execution, and self-checking procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and all six appendix prompts are retained. Evaluating DeepSeek as another base model does not establish a procedural modification.

E1.justification: G-REAL expands from three tasks to four by adding Target Navigation, a shortest-path task with noisy text and implicit graph structure. This extends the input conditions beyond the existing NLGraph shortest-path evaluation. The previous G-REAL, GraCoRe, and NLGraph tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DeepSeek-V3-660B under direct and CoT prompting, plus OWL and GraphTeam using GPT-4o-mini. These introduce evaluated general-purpose and graph-specific multi-agent competitors, substantially expanding comparison beyond v1's individual LLM baselines. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds a DeepSeek-based MA-GTS configuration and several distinct evaluation protocols. Appendix D tests TSP and coloring at 25, 30, 35, and 40 nodes with five instances per size, and measures end-to-end runtime on five randomly selected 15-node TSP graphs. These extend the experimental design; the original accuracy definition remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6.7 adds repeated-query stability analysis, while Appendix D adds larger-graph scalability tests and runtime comparisons. The node-size plot also gains the new G-REAL shortest-path task. These substantially extend the analyses beyond v1's size sweep and layer ablations; Table 4's original ablation results are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-query uncertainty analysis. v2 reports five queries per selected problem and gives per-query accuracy, variance, standard deviation, and mean in Table 5. This introduces statistical reporting for a supplementary experiment, without adding uncertainty estimates to the main comparison table or establishing increased repetitions of its experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new task, baselines, base model, and supplementary analyses. MA-GTS with GPT-4o-mini scores 91.7% on G-REAL shortest path; its six original Table 2 scores remain unchanged. The abstract's G-REAL average changes from 94.2% to 93.6% because task coverage expands. Reported o3-mini NLGraph cycle scores change from 98.9% for both prompting methods to 97.3% direct and 97.8% CoT.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), Algorithm 1's mathematical relationships, and the appendix's algorithm-complexity descriptions are retained. The new opening of Section 3 restates the existing setup; no substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, proofs, or derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims robust performance with both closed- and open-source base models. The introduction and conclusion extend the comparison claim explicitly to existing multi-agent frameworks. The central contributions—MA-GTS, G-REAL, and agent collaboration for graph problem solving—remain the same.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds a rationale for studying 8–25-node graphs based on semantic difficulty and interprets the new experiments as supporting scalability and runtime efficiency. Section 6.7 adds a stability interpretation. Section 3.3 also softens 'optimal or near-optimal' solutions to 'suitable' solutions. The dedicated limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 9 adds the specific DeepSeek-V3-0324-660B version and its access link. The abstract now explicitly states that G-REAL is released alongside MA-GTS. Existing agent prompts, knowledge-base examples, and algorithm-library examples are retained; these disclosures do not establish an underlying implementation change.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands through discussion of OWL, GCoder, GraphAgent, ProGraph, GraphArena, and GLBench. Appendix E and Table 8 add an explicit benchmark comparison concerning noise, naming, contamination, and data generation. DeepSeek and CoT references are added, while Anim-Director is removed. The expansion makes competing graph and multi-agent approaches substantially more central to the positioning.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introduction, condenses several agent descriptions, and adds an introductory notation overview in Section 3. It also updates affiliations and corresponding-author information and adds acknowledgments. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a motivation figure and substantially redraws the architecture diagram. Dataset, performance, and cost tables gain columns or rows, and the node-size plot gains another curve. Four new tables present stability, larger-graph results, runtime, and benchmark characteristics. Appendix figures and the model-details table are also rearranged, while their retained content remains identifiable.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is Table 2's addition of OWL and GraphTeam with the same GPT-4o-mini base, addressing v1's important absence of evaluated multi-agent competitors. The second base model and new stability and scalability experiments further strengthen assessment of the framework's applicability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: supplementary samples are small, the above-90% claims need qualification given the new results, and the runtime-advantage interpretation overlooks OWL's shorter time in Table 7 (139.39 versus 148.48 seconds).
